d: Land of the long white cloud. The generally accepted Māori name for New Zealand. Traditionally the Māori had no actual name for the country it's only since a popular Pākehā story took hold that the Māori adopted the story and has since received popular use.

(Pronounced batch) A small cabin, usually found at a beach or lake side settlement. The origins name goes back to a time when the workforce was predominately male and factories employed large numbers of staff. The name now is a shortened version of bachelor's house that was common for single men to live in when working for the factories. Over time some of these cabins were relocated to scenic places to be used as holiday homes. Now these 'baches' can be anything from small rustic buildings to new modern homes.
Friendly term of endearment for a man

Department Of Conservation (DOC) was formed as a Government entity to look after the Governments held conservation land and interests. In 1987 three entities were merged (Department of Lands and Survey, the Forest Service and the Wildlife Service) to form DOC. DOC has continued and worked on programs started within its parents as well as picking up new programs as required. DOC look after the National Parks, they issue permits and accommodation (hut) fees as well as their conservation programs.
Posture dance, commonly thought of as a war dance, but not specifically.

Meal cooked in an earth oven. Although today to get the same effect cheaper quicker and easier an urn style cooker has been invented and often commercial companies uses these to feed large numbers more efficiently. A traditional hangi will take all day to prepare.
The ancestral homelands of the Māori people. Believed to be Rarotonga (Cook Islands).
The spiritual land of which the spirits of the deceased travel to in the afterlife.
Pressing of noses, part of a traditional hand shake.
Big family group – like the Scottish clan

Rubber slip in sandals. The rest of the world call these flip-flops or Australia calls them thongs. If we go back to the 1940s and New Zealand businessman Anthony Yock, was importing a plastic version of the Japanese sandal - zori. That he called the Japanese Sandal. Production changed to rubber and they were TradeMarked by Morris Yock as Jandals (Ja (panese Sa) ndals). Morris Yock another New Zealand businessman.
Breath of life. Has reference to the creation of wahine by Tāne. Is a blessing but is used as a informal greeting and affirmation example-thank you.
A native flightless bird and our national icon. It’s also what we call ourselves – New Zealanders are Kiwis. (The fruit is a kiwifruit.)

The grass area in front of the wharetupuna/wharenui. The literal meaning alone is rarely the used. When a marae is referred to it has become to mean, including the wharetupuna or wharenui and associated buildings.
Hand held club, sharp on at least one edge

Māori village, specifically the fortified part of the village. The traditional Māori village was laid out like a medieval village as there was the greater village that most of the time people lived in and traded in, the middle a fortified wall surrounding the centre of the village. If the village is attacked the residents retreated behind the fortifications and tried to hold out the attackers.
People non-Māori usually of European descent. Considered to derive from a pre-European word pakepakeha meaning mythical light beings.
Hand held club, round or blunted edges
Short for "Sweet as a nut". Is an old English phrase meaning - everything is good. Due to the New Zealand accent is often misheard, note the second word is "as".
Magical serpent, usually water based but not always.
Treasure, usually referred to in sense of a gift. Can be a physical thing (i.e. hei tiki) as well as non physical (i.e. language, idea passed on)
Sacred - usually breaking tapu has fatal consequences
The nations Government. This is a loose explanation as it has many legal meanings depending on time in history or reference.
Witch doctor – experts in sacred law
Vehicle of transport, usually a canoe
Ancestral house, Sometimes called meeting house
Big building, Sometimes called meeting house
